title: Reylo Type Defs 0.1.1
description: What introspecting one SQL statement returns, and the type of each parameter and column in it: which values each slot can hold. The format's reference is at https://reylo.dev/typedefs.

Type.description: A type: which values a slot can hold. A union or an intersection lists its members in this order, and a new kind is appended, so the order never changes.

label.description: The source's own name for the type, less the modifiers its fields state: `numeric` for `numeric(10,2)`, `varchar` for `varchar(255)`. A database's name is in the dialect the document states at its top, and a type a schema defines is qualified (`public.mood`), which makes the label its identity. Absent on a type the source builds, such as the struct of a `json_build_object`. It never changes what the type means; generators and drivers may key conventions on it.

comment.description: The comment the source keeps on a named type, such as `COMMENT ON TYPE`. A field's own comment is on the field.

title.description: A short name for the type, written for a reader, as JSON Schema's `title`: `Mailing address`, on a type whose `label` is `public.address`. Like the comment, it says nothing of the values.

InclusivelyBounded.description: Inclusive bounds on an integer's values, in its canonical text, as JSON Schema's `minimum` and `maximum` are. Every bound on a whole number has an inclusive spelling (`x > 0` is `min: "1"`), so an integer takes no exclusive bound. Bounds narrow its values only beyond what its width implies.

Bounded.description: Bounds on an ordered kind's finite values, in its canonical text (`"-1.50"`, `"2026-10-23"`), as JSON Schema's `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum` and `exclusiveMaximum` are. A side takes one of its two fields. A bound is written as the constraint states it, so `x > 0` on a decimal of scale 2 is `exclusive_min: "0"`, never `min: "0.01"`. Whether infinity, -infinity and NaN occur is said by the `infinity` and `nan` flags alone, whatever the bounds.

Size.description: How long a value is, in whole numbers of its kind's unit (bytes, elements, a map's keys, or a text's `unit`): `exact`, or `min`, `max` or both. A length is never exclusive, since a whole number has an inclusive spelling.

IntegerType.description: A whole number of a fixed width, two's complement unless `unsigned`: 32 bits for a typical `int`, 128 for a `hugeint`. Its range follows from the width, and bounds narrow it further, as for a year held in 16 bits and kept to 1901 to 2155. An integer of no fixed width is a `decimal` whose scale is at most 0.

FloatType.description: An IEEE 754 binary float, given by its exponent and mantissa widths, which fix its range and precision: a double is 11 and 52, a single 8 and 23, a half 5 and 10, and a bfloat16 8 and 7. A width alone would not do, since those last two are both 16 bits. A generator picks the smallest native float whose widths are both at least these. -0 is a float like any other, and equal to 0.

mantissa_bits.description: Not counting the implicit leading bit.

DecimalType.description: An exact decimal: a coefficient, a whole number, times a power of ten (1.25 is 125 × 10^-2). It is a kind of its own, so that a generator switching on the kind never turns money into a float. SQL counts the power negated, as the scale, the digits after the point, and a type bounds both: `numeric(10,2)` has precision 10 and scale 2, so it holds up to 99,999,999.99. A decimal is a number, so 1.5 and 1.50 are one value however a source prints them.

precision.description: The most digits in the coefficient.

min_scale.description: A value is in the type when it can be written as a coefficient of at most `precision` digits times 10^-scale, with a scale from `min_scale` to `max_scale`: precision 5 and scale 2 to 2 hold 1.5, written 150 × 10^-2. Equal bounds make a fixed scale; a negative scale rounds to tens, hundreds and so on.

TextType.description: Text. With no `encoding`, its values are any valid Unicode text: sequences of Unicode scalar values. An `encoding` names the character set its values are held in, so every character is one that set can encode, and, with `ill_formed`, its values may be any sequence of that set's code units, valid or not. `code_points` narrows the characters further. How text compares, under a collation, is not part of its type, since how a source compares text changes no value.

encoding.description: The character set the values are held in, by its IANA name, pinned to one mapping table (spec/README.md): every character is one it encodes. A Unicode encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32, CESU-8, GB18030) encodes every character, so it is written only beside `ill_formed`, or where a size counts its code units or bytes.

ill_formed.description: Values may be any sequence of the encoding's code units, not only valid text: bytes for UTF-8 or a single-byte set, 16-bit units for UTF-16 (a lone surrogate), 32-bit units up to 0x10FFFF for UTF-32. Written only beside `encoding`.

code_points.description: Inclusive ranges of code points every character falls in, beside what `encoding` allows: `[[1, 1114111]]` holds no NUL, `[[0, 65535]]` nothing past the Basic Multilingual Plane. Sorted, disjoint and never adjacent. In ill-formed text, a lone surrogate or a 32-bit unit is held to them by its value.

pattern.description: An I-Regexp (RFC 9485) every value matches whole: `[^@]+@[^@]+`. Matched against ill-formed text as decoded, each ill-formed sequence read as U+FFFD.

media_type.description: What the text is, as a media type (`text/html`): JSON Schema's `contentMediaType`.

format.description: What the text is meant to be, by JSON Schema's format name (`email`, `uri`, `hostname`, `ipv4`) or a source's own. It is a name alone, which says nothing of the values: a rule every value keeps is written as a `pattern`. A consumer that does not know a format ignores it. A format the format has a kind for is written as that kind: `date-time` is an `instant`, `uuid` a `uuid` and `binary` `bytes`.

TextSize.description: A text's length: in code points where `unit` is absent, in the encoding's code units (UTF-16 units, as a JavaScript string's `length` counts), or in bytes in the encoding. A unit other than code points is written only where the text names its `encoding`.

Charset.description: A character set, by its IANA name, matched without regard to case: the Unicode encodings; US-ASCII and ISO 8859, pinned to Unicode's mapping tables; the Windows code pages, pinned to the WHATWG Encoding Standard's indexes; and the sets databases and languages still store.

BytesType.description: Bytes: any sequence of octets, of the size it states. Its canonical text is base64 (RFC 4648, padded).

media_type.description: What the bytes are, as a media type (`image/png`): JSON Schema's `contentMediaType`.

UuidType.description: A 128-bit identifier, in RFC 9562's text form. It holds any 128 bits, the nil UUID and bits no RFC version describes among them, unless `versions` says otherwise.

versions.description: Every value is of RFC 9562's variant, with one of these versions: `[7]`, or all eight for any RFC UUID. Written only where the source guarantees it.

EnumType.description: One of a fixed list of values of `type`, in that type's canonical text: an enum's labels, a `CHECK (x IN (…))`, or a constant a statement writes. An enum of one value is a literal: `select 'user' as kind` is `{ kind: "enum", type: { kind: "text" }, values: ["user"] }`. The list's order is the source's, and how its values sort is not part of the type.

type.description: A kind whose values the format writes as text: a boolean (`"true"`), a number, text, bytes, a UUID, a date, a time or a duration. Never itself an enum.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value. Bounds constrain only the finite values.

TimeType.description: A time of day. Its `max` may be `24:00:00`, which some languages' time types refuse.

offset.description: Each value keeps a UTC offset beside the time.

DateTimeType.description: A date and a time of day as a wall clock reads them, with no zone: no moment until a zone is given.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value. Bounds constrain only the finite values.

InstantType.description: A point on the timeline and nothing else, as Temporal's `Instant`: written in UTC (`2026-11-14T18:14:00Z`). A source that prints one with an offset adds the offset as it prints. Bounds are in UTC.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value. Bounds constrain only the finite values.

ZonedDateTimeType.description: A point on the timeline and the time zone it was written in, a region or a UTC offset, as Temporal's `ZonedDateTime`: written as RFC 9557 does, `2026-11-14T10:14:00-08:00[America/Los_Angeles]`, or `2026-11-14T10:14:00-08:00[-08:00]` for an offset. Bounds compare the moments.

offset_only.description: Every value's zone is a UTC offset, never a region, as Java's `OffsetDateTime`.

infinity.description: Also holds infinity and -infinity, which sort after and before every other value. Bounds constrain only the finite values.

DurationType.description: A length of time, in the parts it has (months, days and time), each signed on its own. A month and a day have no fixed length (a month is 28 to 31 days, and a day 23 to 25 hours across a clock change), so a duration that counts them keeps them apart from its time. ISO 8601's intervals, a start and an end, are a `range` here.

max.description: The parts its values have, each at the largest magnitude it reaches, of either sign, as one ISO 8601 duration: months in `M`, days in `D`, then time in `H`, `M` and `S`, its minutes and seconds below 60. A part the type lacks is left out, and a part it has is never 0. A two's complement part reaches one unit further below zero than above it, so it is written at the negative side's magnitude: 32-bit months are `2147483648M`.

tick.description: The time part's smallest step, written exactly when `max` has a time part.

ArrayType.description: A sequence of elements, in order, each in the one `element` slot. An array is flat: a two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, each level of its own. Where its index starts is not part of it. Its size counts its elements, so a vector of 3 floats is `size: { exact: 3 }`, and a bit string an array of booleans of its length.

distinct.description: No two elements are equal, by the source's own equality, and so no two are the same value: a set, as JSON Schema's `uniqueItems` says.

TupleType.description: A sequence of values, each of its own type, with no names: `[1, "a"]`. `elements` come first and are always there, `optional_elements` follow, each present only where the one before it is, and `rest` takes any number after them. JSON Schema writes the same with `prefixItems`, `minItems` and `items`.

elements.description: The elements every value has, in order.

optional_elements.description: Elements that may be missing from the end, in order: a value with the second of them has the first.

rest.description: Any number of further elements, each in this slot.

StructType.description: Named fields, in order: a row, a composite type, an object. A struct holds exactly its fields, unless `extra` lets it hold other keys too. A source's sugar over simpler values is a struct carrying its `label`, as a point is `{ x, y }`.

extra.description: Keys beyond its fields, any number, each holding a value in this slot, as JSON Schema's `additionalProperties`: it says nothing of the named fields. A key is text, and none is a field's name.

MapType.description: Keys to values, each key once and in no order: a dictionary. A map whose keys may repeat is an array of `{ key, value }` structs. Its size counts its keys, as JSON Schema's `minProperties` and `maxProperties` do.

key.description: Inside JSON content, a key is text and never null.

TableType.description: Rows of columns: what a statement returns, and a table nested in a value, such as SQL's `MULTISET`. A row of a table is a struct of its columns; a language may hold a table as an array of objects, a list of tuples, or columns.

cardinality.description: How many rows: exactly one, at most one, any number, or none (a write that returns nothing).

columns.description: In order; empty where there are no rows.

unique.description: Each set of columns, by name, no two rows agree on all of: no two equal under the source's own equality, a null equal to another null, and so no two the same values. None inside another: `[["id"], ["email"]]`. A column of a unique index counts only where its nulls cannot repeat. Only where the cardinality is `many`.

order.description: The columns the rows are sorted on, in order, by the source's own sort, as far as the sort names columns of the table: `order by at desc, lower(name), id` gives only `at`, since its next key is no column, and `id` then sorts only rows that tie. A key under another collation than its column's ends the list. Rows that tie on all of them come in any order. Only where the cardinality is `many`.

SortKey.description: A column a table's rows are sorted on.

desc.description: Sorted from the highest value down.

JsonType.description:
A JSON value.
  - `content`: what a statement built, described with the same types, each leaf typed by the value it was written from, so a 64-bit integer may pass 2^53.
  - `schema`: a JSON Schema every value satisfies, whose `$schema` names the draft it is read by.
  - Neither: any JSON, whose numbers may have any length.

content.description: Where it may be null, the document may be JSON null.

UnionType.description: One of several types: each value is one of them. A union whose values say which member they are is a `tagged_union`.

IntersectionType.description: Values of every member at once: JSON Schema's `allOf`, TypeScript's `&`. An intersection one struct can write, of structs whose fields agree or of a struct and a map with text keys, is written as that struct.

TaggedUnionType.description: One of several alternatives, each named by the tag every value carries, in the order the type declares them, as a Rust enum. Unlike a union's members, two alternatives may hold one type, and a value says which alternative it is even where it holds null.

Alternative.description: An alternative of a tagged union: its tag, unique in the type, and the slot of the value it holds.

RangeType.description: A range of `subtype`, with an empty range and unbounded ends: a start and an end. Over a discrete subtype, such as integers or dates, `[1,3]` and `[1,4)` are one range. An unbounded end lies beyond the subtype's infinities, so `[x,)` holds infinity and `[x,infinity)` does not.

MultirangeType.description: An ordered set of non-overlapping ranges.

GeometryType.description: An OGC simple feature, planar or on a spheroid (`geodetic`).

XmlType.description: XML: a document with one root, valid against any `schemas` given, or a fragment, which may have several roots (`<a/><b/>`). An XML Schema validates documents only, so a fragment names none.

NullType.description: The value that is always null, in a slot marked `nullable`: the field of a `json_build_object('a', null)`.

OpaqueType.description: A type the source knows and the format does not structure: an extension's own type, or one that holds a value of any type, each carrying its own. Its `label` is all the format says; what a value looks like is the driver's to decide.

UnknownType.description: Nothing is known about the values, but whether one may be null, which its slot says.

StatementDescriptor.description: What introspecting one statement returns. A tool may write keys of its own beside these, as `reylo analyze` writes the file a statement was read from.

$schema.description: The version of the format the descriptor is written in, as the URL of that version's JSON Schema, which a validator or an editor reads. Versions are semantic, and until 1.0.0 a new minor version may change anything.

sql.description: The statement as the database runs it, with its own placeholders (`$1` on Postgres, `?` on MySQL and SQLite), in the order `params` lists them.

kind.description: `select` for any query, a `VALUES` list and a set operation included; `other` for any statement that is none of the five: a `CALL`, whose procedure may write, an `EXPLAIN`, a `SHOW` or a SQLite `PRAGMA`, and DDL. Absent when the statement does not parse.

comment.description: The prose written in comments before the statement: its summary, as an editor's hover shows it.

result.description: What the statement returns, a table: a row of columns per row, and its cardinality. A statement that returns one value is still a row of one column, which keeps the column's name. A row is an object keyed by its columns' names, which keeps only the last of two with one name, so a statement whose result repeats a name (`select a.id, b.id`) has a diagnostic at each later column of it, asking for another name with `as`. The name the database gives a column stands: Postgres calls `select 1`'s `?column?`.

capabilities.description: What running the statement may do, an upper bound: a flag it lacks, or a table it does not name, is something it cannot do, so a statement whose tables are all `read` and that has no flag only reads. Absent, nothing is said.

diagnostics.description: What the database or the introspection reports against the statement, each at its place, so an editor can underline it. A statement that does not parse has a diagnostic and no columns.

Diagnostic.description: `start` and `end` are offsets into the statement as it was written, in UTF-16 units, as the Language Server Protocol counts by default. `code` is the database's own error code where it has one (Postgres's SQLSTATE `42703`, MySQL's `1054`).

Slot.description: Where a type is used: a column, a parameter, a struct's field, an array's element, a tuple's element, a map's key or value, a tagged union's alternative, JSON content. Whether a value may be null is the slot's to say, never the type's, so one type reads the same at every use. A union's members, an intersection's, an enum's type and a range's subtype are bare types, since a value stands at none of them.

nullable.description: The value may be null, whatever the type's values, bounds or label say. On a parameter, the statement accepts null; inside JSON content, the value may be JSON null.

Field.description: A struct's field or a table's column: a key of an object, a column of a row.

optional.description: The key may be absent, apart from whether its value may be null; `default` names the value it takes where it is absent.

default.description: The value an optional field takes where its key is absent, in its type's canonical text: only beside `optional`.

comment.description: What the field is, as its source documents it, such as the comment a database keeps on a column.

title.description: A short name for the field, as JSON Schema's `title`.

Param.description: A statement's parameter. Where the statement writes it whole into a column, its type is that column's: `insert into t (price) values (:price)` into a decimal of scale 2 gives `price` that scale, though the database describes the parameter with none and would round 1.234. That is stricter than the server, never looser.

optional.description: The caller may leave the parameter out.

comment.description: The comment the database keeps on the column the parameter is written to whole.

Dialect.description: The database a document of descriptors describes, stated once at the document's top: every `label` inside is this dialect's. `name` is the database's, such as `postgres`, `mysql`, `sqlite`, `duckdb`, `oracle` or `sqlserver`, and `version` its server version.

Capabilities.description: What running a statement may do: the tables it touches, and four kinds of effect beyond their rows.

tables.description: Each table the statement touches, qualified as a `label` is (`public.posts`), with the most it may do to its rows, through a view, a partition, a foreign key's action or a sequence's default too; `unknown` where it may touch tables the analysis cannot name, as through a function or a trigger whose body it does not read.

ddl.description: Creates, alters or drops what the database defines, or changes who may use it: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `GRANT`.

transaction.description: Begins or ends a transaction: `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `SAVEPOINT`, and MySQL's DDL, which commits.

session.description: Leaves state on the connection after it: `SET`, a temporary table, a session's advisory lock, `PREPARE`, `LISTEN`, MySQL's `USE`, a SQLite `PRAGMA` or `ATTACH`.

external.description: Reaches past the connection and the data: the server's settings (`ALTER SYSTEM`, `SET GLOBAL`), another session (`NOTIFY`, ending a backend), a file or the network.

Access.description: The most a statement may do to a table's rows, each covering the ones before it: `read`; `readlock`, which reads them and locks them until its transaction ends (`FOR UPDATE`, `LOCK TABLE`); and `write`, which inserts, updates or deletes them.
